analysis.one_liner: Boosts Obamacare plans so they cover more of people's medical bills.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in January 2026 by Rep. Kim Schrier with one cosponsor, has sat with two House committees since the day it was introduced, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make health plans sold on the Affordable Care Act marketplaces cover a bigger share of people's medical bills, starting in 2028. It would raise the plan's share of costs to as much as 94% for lower- and middle-income enrollees, extend that richer coverage to people earning up to four times the poverty line, and base premium subsidies on 'gold' plans instead of cheaper, skimpier 'silver' plans. It pays for the extra help out of general federal funds.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage through the ACA marketplaces, especially households earning roughly 150% to 400% of the federal poverty line. Starting in 2028 they would face much lower deductibles and out-of-pocket limits: plans would have to cover 87% to 94% of allowed costs for those groups, up from today's roughly 70% to 87%. People currently eligible for cost-sharing help would get richer 'gold-level' coverage instead of silver, and premium subsidies would be calculated against gold plans, making fuller coverage affordable with little or no premium for many.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ACA marketplace enrollees with modest incomes

how_it_helps.text: For plan years starting on or after January 1, 2028, cost-sharing reductions would be calculated as if enrollees had gold-level coverage rather than silver, meaning the plan pays a larger share of medical bills.

The bill extends the richest cost-sharing help (plans covering 87% of costs) to households earning up to 300% of the poverty line, and gives households between 300% and 400% of poverty plans covering 85% of costs, eligibility these households lack today.
Premium tax credits would be calculated using the second-lowest-cost gold plan rather than the silver plan, so the subsidy benchmark would buy fuller coverage.
State Basic Health Program benchmark plans would shift to gold-level coverage on the same schedule.
The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' from the Treasury for the added cost-sharing payments.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The added cost-sharing payments and the larger premium credits that come from benchmarking subsidies to gold plans would come from general Treasury funds with no dedicated revenue source, so the bill adds to federal deficits.

drawbacks.text: The bill is funded by an open-ended appropriation with no dedicated revenue or offset, so it adds directly to federal deficits by however much the richer coverage costs.
The richer coverage does not start until 2028, and the bill does not address the enhanced premium tax credits that expire sooner, leaving many enrollees' premium costs to jump in the meantime.

Gold-level plans carry higher premiums than the silver plans today's subsidies are built around, so the federal cost per enrollee rises and insurers collect larger federal payments; the money flows through private insurers rather than any public option.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and large: marketplace enrollees at these incomes today can face deductibles of several thousand dollars, and this would sharply cut that exposure. The honest cost is that it is expensive and entirely deficit-financed, and it routes the money through private insurers, whose premiums rise along with the richer benefits. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on federal borrowing against directly cutting families' medical bills.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced and has not moved since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the bill on January 20, 2026, joined by Rep. Nikki Budzinski.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and also to the Ways and Means Committee, the standard two-track referral that splits jurisdiction over ACA provisions and the tax code.
The bill has one cosponsor, Rep. Budzinski, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, because nothing has happened. The practical effect so far is the status quo: marketplace enrollees at 300% to 400% of poverty still face deductibles and cost-sharing the bill would have reduced, and private insurers continue collecting premiums tied to today's thinner silver-level coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, nobody — the status quo holds

for.name: Rep. Kim Schrier
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand ACA cost-sharing reductions and shift the subsidy benchmark to gold plans.

for.name: Rep. Nikki Budzinski
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed it on the record, but support is limited to two House Democrats and no Republican has signed on, and the bill has not reached a vote that would reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would channel larger federal cost-sharing payments and higher-premium gold-plan subsidies through private marketplace insurers, locking them in as the permanent delivery system for ACA coverage while requiring them to cover a bigger share of costs. Consumers get lower out-of-pocket bills at the same time insurers get bigger, federally funded revenue — the two rise together.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with two committees and no second cosponsor, with no hearing scheduled. Most House bills introduced this way never reach the floor, and health subsidy expansions face a difficult path in a closely divided Congress, so the realistic outlook is that it dies in committee unless its sponsors attach the idea to larger health legislation.
